## [One swell foop](https://seths.blog/2026/11/one-swell-foop-2/)

It’s definitely tempting. All at once. Once and done. Over with.

Pay the money, grit your teeth, launch with verve and then move on.

Except…

it almost never works.

Foops aren’t swell. Foops fail.

The successful path is a process, an iterative, evolving, persistent path toward better.

November 18, 2026

title: Can Science Save the Ice Skaters?
content:
_“It giet oan,”_ Henk Kroes, veteran “ice master,” told a room full of reporters on January 2, 1997: “It is happening.”

Kroes was referring to the _Elfstedentocht_, a 125-mile ice skating competition in the northern Netherlands province of Friesland. For more than a century, the race has been as much a competition as a national celebration. “Never am I happier,” wrote the 17th-century playwright and skating enthusiast Gerbrand Bredero, “as when I am gliding over ice.” The feeling was passed down over the ages in the Netherlands.

The racecourse circles through 11 picturesque Friesland cities. It takes skaters across lakes, winding rivers, and canals. It begins with 300 speed skaters competing for the trophy, followed by an unruly train of nearly 20,000 leisure skaters in their wake.

Kroes, who at the time served as chairman of the Royal Association of the Friesian Eleven Cities, was expressing a mix of relief and excitement.

Race officials had just reported that the ice was 6 inches thick, just barely meeting the minimum safety requirements for the event to proceed. If the ice was any thinner, it wouldn’t hold the weight of the skaters. For years, race officials had worried that sections of the course wouldn’t freeze at all.

Today in the Netherlands Kroes’ words—spoken in his native Frisian dialect—mostly inspire a nostalgic sadness. Due to global warming, there has not been another official _Elfstedentocht_ since 1997. And climate scientists say it is becoming increasingly unlikely that we will ever see one again.

**SLIP SLIDIN’ AWAY:** A lone skater glides over a reed-fringed canal in Friesland, home of the traditional Elfstedentocht skating tour. _Credit: 365 Focus Photography / Shutterstock_

The biggest natural ice-skating competition in the world, the first _Elfstedentocht_ was held in 1909. It almost immediately became one of the most beloved sporting events in the country, rivaling professional football. Perhaps the most iconic iteration of the race—and one that feels especially far removed from the situation today—was the so-called “Hell of ‘63,” when strong winds and temperatures low enough to freeze eyelids kept nearly 99 percent of the nearly 10,000 participants from reaching the finish line.

Frisians in particular remember not just the bitter cold, but also the warmth of their own community. Throughout the 20th century, ordinary economic activity in the province froze to a halt whenever a race was imminent, while the monotony and drudgery of ordinary life melted away like snow in the sun.

Archeological evidence suggests that people living in the Netherlands have been skating across ice in some capacity since the days of the Roman Empire, whose northern border stopped just short of Friesland’s southern edge. During the late Middle Ages, when Dutch winters grew colder as a result of a regional cooling period sometimes referred to as the Little Ice Age, frozen rivers turned into highways, keeping towns connected as land routes became all but impassable. As documented by painters like Pieter Bruegel the Elder and Hendrick Avercamp, skating also proved a popular pastime, enjoyed by peasants and aristocrats alike.

According to the Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute, which issues weather forecasts and studies climate trends, the number of ice days—a 24-hour period where the maximum air temperature remains below 32 degrees F—has been declining ever since the 1960s, from an average of 11 per year to just 3. The average temperature of ice days has also been increasing: Entire days that remained below 14 degrees F, once relatively common, have not occurred since 1987 in the Netherlands.

As winters warm, a skill that was once as common and culturally definitive to the Dutch identity as cycling is set to fade away while the _Elfstedentocht_ transforms from a living tradition into a bittersweet memory of colder, happier days.

Unwilling to accept the climatic erosion of a cultural institution, the Netherlands’ brightest science and engineering minds have sought solutions that could preserve the national pastime with a triptych of ingenious ways to fool Mother Nature and get skaters back on the ice.

But using brute technological force to create conditions cold enough to sustain ice is highly impractical. The _Elfstedentocht_’s waters cannot be cooled the way we cool artificial ice rinks. In 2021, Dutch newspaper _De Volkskrant_ reported that the 720 diesel-powered industrial-grade chillers needed to do so—though comparatively cheap at a “sponsorable” €90 million—would pump so much CO 2 into the atmosphere (more than 17,000 tons) that it would be more sustainable to fly all 30,000 preregistered contestants (members of the Royal Association of the Friesian Eleven Cities) with their skates at the ready to a lake in the Austrian Alps.

A more sustainable option would be to cover the surface of the water with what is called passive radiative cooling film. Inspired by the heat-resistant hairs of Saharan silver ants, which survive in temperatures up to 150 degrees F, this film is lined with miniscule pockets that scatter and reflect more than 95 percent of visible and UV light, while also emitting infrared light at wavelengths that allow it to pass through greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.

As its name implies, passive radiative cooling film works passively, exchanging heat without consuming energy and therefore shrinking the bill down to the costs of the material itself and the labor needed to deploy it. But while an experiment by Nick van de Giesen, an engineer at Delft University of Technology, has shown that this film can indeed be used for growing ice, its ability to do so is heavily dependent on the weather. Most effective in hot, dry climates—as in silver ants’ native range—the material does not work nearly as well in the cloudy, humid conditions typical of Friesland, since water vapor prevents infrared light from escaping.

Van de Giesen says that, rather than covering the entirety of the _Elfstedentocht_’s route, cooling film could be deployed in specific areas where ice formation occurs more slowly, such as underneath the 194 bridges that dot the course. Normally preventing the stored heat from rising up into the cooled night sky, in this scenario they could instead protect the film from rain and snowfall.

An even more ambitious idea, proposed by fellow TU Delft professor Andy van den Dobbelsteen, is to facilitate ice growth using aquathermal energy-powered heat pumps.

A technology whose development dates back all the way to the early 19th century, aquathermal heat pumps can heat homes and businesses by extracting heat from a body of water, such as wastewater or—as Van den Dobbelsteen proposes—natural surface waters. For heating, the source water is brought into contact with a conductive tube containing a refrigerant: a chemical compound with an unusually low boiling point. As dictated by the second law of thermodynamics, heat from the warmer source water passes through the tube into the colder refrigerant, causing it to heat up and evaporate. The resulting gas is then compressed, increasing its temperature even further, before being passed along another tube containing the water used to heat a building, which is then warmed just like the refrigerant was before. Finally, the warmed heating water is pumped into radiators for delivery, just like a traditional boiler does. To cool a space, the process runs in reverse: Warmth is extracted from the building’s heating water, then discharged back into the source by way of the refrigerant.

In preparation for a keynote speech at a 2019 sustainable construction congress in Friesland’s provincial capital, Leeuwarden, Van den Dobbelsteen calculated that cooling more than 31.7 million gallons of surface water along the _Elfstedentocht_ route by about 7 degrees Fahrenheit over the course of a single week would require the removal of 40 trillion joules of heat, approximately the amount of electricity that more than 4,500 Dutch households consume in a year. Assuming that a single heat pump has a power capacity of 10 kilowatts (most individual residential models on the market today range between 2 and 20 kW), generating that much energy would require 10,000 pumps, installed along the route at 65.5-foot intervals, with 26 wind turbines to power them.

Though intimidating in scale, Van den Dobbelsteen’s plan has its advantages. While passive radiative cooling film sends solar energy back into space, heat pumps could use that energy to warm buildings here on Earth. Furthermore, if operated in the summer as well as in the winter, the heat pumps could contribute to improving surface water quality by suppressing toxic blue-green algal blooms, which have become increasingly common in natural water bodies in the Netherlands and across the globe as a result of climate change.

Perhaps the biggest advantage of facilitating ice growth using heat pumps—one Van den Dobbelsteen has frequently stressed in public appearances—is that the cost and effort required for their installation and operation can be folded into Friesland’s larger energy transition: an undertaking which was mandated by the Dutch Climate Act’s objective to reach carbon neutrality by 2050. While industrial chillers and cooling film provide no use other than to increase the odds of another _Elfstedentocht_, 10,000 heat pumps deployed along the course would extract enough energy in winter to warm 10 percent of Friesland’s homes, and even more if they were used during other seasons as well.

**LIFE ON ICE:** Canals in the Netherlands, like this one in Alblessardam, become arteries for travel, recreation, and socialization in the winter. _Credit: Christian Badescu / Shutterstock_

Of course, this plan has its problems, too, one of which concerns population density. While many pumps can be directly hooked up to houses and farms along the water, the _Elfstedentocht_ also moves though long stretches of empty countryside where extracted heat would go to waste without storage or distribution—requiring infrastructure which, though certainly useful for Friesland’s energy transition, would also make the project more logistically challenging and costlier. Van den Dobbelsteen has proposed incentivizing private contractors to develop floating vacation rentals, though such a solution would still leave a large number of the 10,000 pumps unaccounted for.

Next, there’s the problem of home insulation. According to the National Programme for Local Heat Transition (NPLW), a government agency in the Netherlands that assists municipalities transitioning away from natural gas, aquathermal heat pumps can provide up to 60 percent of a building’s heat supply—provided the building has a European Union-designated energy label of B or higher. Considering that Friesland ranks among the lower end of home insulation per province, with 21 percent of homes actually bearing a label of D or lower, this means a substantial number of homes would probably require an additional heat source to stay sufficiently warm.

Gerben Jan de Vries, a senior technical advisor at aquathermal consultancy firm WarmteTransitieMakers, whom _Nautilus_ asked to evaluate the feasibility of Van den Dobbelsteen’s plan, doesn’t think this is necessarily an issue, at least not in the long run. “Poorly insulated homes require a lot of energy to stay warm, so there’s a lot of potential for savings,” he says. “Imagine you travel far and often for work, and have to choose between a cheap car that uses a lot of gas, and a more expensive hybrid or electric one. The more you use it, the quicker you earn back that difference.”

The ecological ramifications of the heat pump plan raise another point of contention. Lieke Noij, an independent research coordinator working with Netherlands-based water board innovation center STOWA, says any ecological studies on the impact of such a big heat pump project involve a number of persistent challenges, from controlling for the effects of covariates like weather and traffic to counting the number of living microorganisms after they have passed through a pump filtration system. Still, while many of these questions have yet to be answered in full scientific detail, there is one thing she can already say with relative certainty: Any aquathermal application which manages to alter the temperature of its source water—as the pumps of the _Elfstedentocht_ plan specifically aim to do—will have an effect on the environment. Though capable of curbing harmful algae in summer, a sudden drop in water temperature during the winter, even by a single degree, could interfere with the life cycles of certain animals and springtime plant growth.

Van den Dobbelsteen sees things differently. “Dutch legislation allows companies to discharge wastewater of up to [84.2 degrees F] into Frisian waters,” he says. “And spring season starts earlier than it did in the past.” He adds that cooling down the water is “hardly a disturbance if we are restoring the temperature to what it used to be,” and that if any flora or fauna would suffer as a result, it’s invasive, exotic species—like the American crayfish or the floating pennywort—that would never have been able to live there in the first place were it not for climate change.

Noij admits that setting environmental guidelines for an already warmed and warming planet isn’t straightforward or beyond debate. Moreover, she wishes that the people in charge of approving aquathermal projects would weigh the “societal value” of the energy transition more heavily in their assessments, balancing its immediate costs with long-term gains.

Finally, while using heat pumps to save the ice and revive the _Elfstedentocht_ is more sustainable than turning the route into a diesel-powered ice rink, it may not be the most optimal way that aquathermal energy could be employed. Elsewhere in the Netherlands, such as along Amsterdam’s Jacob van Lennepkanaal, pumps extract heat during the summer rather than in the winter, when water surface temperatures are much warmer, with extracted heat stored underground for use on colder days. Heat extraction during winter is possible, but less efficient: A 2020 report by STOWA warns that temperatures close to freezing can be too cold to extract sufficient warmth, and installations run the risk of being damaged due to frost. Van den Dobbelsteen says this risk is greater in some systems than others, and it can be averted by shutting down the pumps when frost begins to form. But would doing so not defeat the very purpose of the plan?

Van den Dobbelsteen’s idea may not be without its kinks, but it is the most tantalizing of all the ones proposed up to this point. Not a single expert on aquathermal energy that _Nautilus_ spoke to expressed doubts about its theoretical viability. Instead, concerns pointed in the direction of financing, logistics, bureaucracy, and other pragmatic stumbling blocks. It continues to be discussed in Dutch news media, and has attracted the attention of—and received endorsement from—universities, private companies, and government agencies alike.

Interestingly, one organization that has been lukewarm about the idea is the Royal Association of the Friesian Eleven Cities. “Our guiding principle,” spokesperson Wini Weidenaar says, “is that there can only be an _Elfstedentocht_ if nature allows it. We recognize that with climate change the chances get slimmer and slimmer, and are not saying that technology cannot play a role, but we are not about artificially creating a race if nature doesn’t provide us with the right conditions. The uncertainty is part of the magic.”

Here, too, Van den Dobbelsteen would kindly beg to differ. For one, there is a long history of people stepping in to increase the odds of another race, with and without modern tech at their side: by pausing boat traffic, removing fresh, insulating snowfall from the ice so additional heat can continue to escape unobstructed, and performing “ice transplantations” to plug up holes, among other strategies. On top of this, in the Anthropocene, is there even such a thing as “natural” when it comes to weather and climate anymore? “If you want an _Elfstedentocht_ without human interference,” he says, then not only shouldn’t there be one today, but the one in 1997 shouldn’t have happened either, because ever since the Industrial Revolution, “nature has already been disturbed.”

The practical and philosophical questions raised by the _Elfstedentocht_ constitute a double-edged sword, er, skate. On the one hand, technology has led to climate change, which is now threatening traditional ways of life all across the world, from imperiling the reeds used to make the floating Uros islands of Peru’s Lake Titicaca to threatening semi-nomadic Sámi reindeer herders migrating through upper Scandinavia. At the same time, technology often proves the only hope of keeping traditions alive, albeit in inevitably altered states.

A study published earlier this summer, using ice growth models with temperature projections for different emission scenarios, suggests that we should probably count on no more than a single “natural” _Elfstedentocht_ between now and 2100. The odds of this happening are projected to decrease by the decade, though—incredibly—they may one day go up again. At some unknown point in the future, most likely during the next century or possibly this one, climate scientists expect the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation or AMOC, a current that pushes warm water from the southern hemisphere into the North Atlantic, to weaken and perhaps collapse. If this happens, the effects on Europe’s climate may be not unlike those of the Little Ice Age—extreme winter temperatures in the Netherlands could drop to 24.8 degrees F—setting the stage for Dutch ice skating to come sliding back into an uncertain future.

Until then, Van den Dobbelsteen will keep on advocating for his heat pump plan, while the ice masters of the Association—as retired journalist and volunteer at one of Friesland’s many ice skating clubs William Altema put it—continue “praying to the god of winter for winds from icy Siberia.” ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Why Can Some People Lower Their Cholesterol Through Dieting While Others Can’t?
content:
Trying to drive down your cholesterol by changing your diet can be frustrating. You swap out regular bacon for turkey bacon, eat more oatmeal, and at the end of the day it might not even make a dent in your LDL levels. And yet, dietary interventions seem to work wonders for some people. While it’s tempting to chalk up stubborn cholesterol numbers to genetics, a new study published in the _Journal of the American College of Cardiology_ is complicating the picture.

“We have people who come into the clinic and say, ‘I changed my diet, and it made no difference in my cholesterol,’” study author Shoa Clarke of Stanford University said in a [statement](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1151889). “Or they say, ‘I changed my diet, and it had a huge effect on my cholesterol.’”

**Read more: “**[**Iron Is the New Cholesterol**](https://nautil.us/iron-is-the-new-cholesterol-237280)**”**

To find out why, Clarke and a team of medical researchers examined health data from a diverse group of nearly 21,000 postmenopausal women enrolled in the Women’s Health Initiative, a longitudinal national health study launched in 1991 that collected genetic profiles, dietary questionnaires, and blood lipid panels from the participants. Using a polygenic risk score [established](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-021-04064-3) in a prior study, they found that those with a greater genetic predisposition to higher cholesterol were also more sensitive to saturated fat intake.

“Sometimes people think, ‘Oh, if I’m genetically prone to something, then it doesn’t really matter what my diet is or what the environment is like; it’s genetically predetermined.’ But what we’re saying here is the opposite,” Clarke explained. “The people who had this genetic predisposition for higher LDL were actually the ones with the most sensitivity to diet, where diet has the best chance of helping them—or hurting them, if the diet isn’t good.”

When the team looked at the incidence of adverse cardiovascular events among the women, the same pattern emerged. The top 25 percent of participants with a genetic bent toward high LDL levels who consumed more saturated fat were also more likely to suffer a heart attack, stroke, or other adverse cardiovascular event. The saturated fat intake for the remaining 75 percent didn’t seem to matter as much. “This variation in response to saturated fat may be one of the reasons there is so much controversy and disagreement over how much is okay in a diet,” Clarke said.

Of course, the study comes with some fine print. The food questionnaires were only given once, covering a three-month period in a longer study, so it’s entirely possible they changed over time. Additionally, only postmenopausal women were studied. The outcomes for men or women of different ages may vary.

But the bottom line is a familiar one (with a twist): reducing saturated fat is good for your LDL levels, especially if you’re genetically prone to high cholesterol. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Save the Parasites!
content:
_[This story](https://knowablemagazine.org/content/article/living-world/2026/save-the-parasites) was originally published by_[Knowable Magazine](https://knowablemagazine.org/content/article/society/2026/prehistory-lost-threads)_._

In the 1980s, biologists rounded up every last California condor for captive breeding. It was an unprecedented conservation project with stunning success: Today, the birds [number more than 600](https://www.fws.gov/sites/default/files/documents/2026-02/2025-california-condor-population-status_508-compliant.pdf).

But for some ecologists, there’s a distressing corollary: The [birds](https://knowablemagazine.org/content/article/food-environment/2025/california-condor-reintroduction) were reportedly treated with pesticides that killed condor parasites, including one [unique to these birds](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/canadian-entomologist/article/abs/species-of-colpocephalum-mallophaga-menoponidae-parasitic-upon-the-falconiformes1/4496DA09717B6B91C5B752E1D27B440B), the condor louse _Colpocephalum californici_. The condor louse became a poster child for parasite extinction.

Parasites have a bad rap. But parasite ecologists say most parasitic species don’t harm us or our domestic animals and, in fact, make important contributions to life on Earth.

Amid today’s rapidly changing ecosystems, not much is known about how most parasites are faring: Better? Worse? The same? But by one estimate, climate-induced loss of habitat could cause [extinction for 5 to 10 percent of parasite species](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.1602422) by 2070. In 2023, the International Union for Conservation of Nature — the group responsible for the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species — [started a new parasite specialist group](https://iucn.org/our-union/commissions/group/iucn-ssc-parasite-specialist-group), which aims to red-list more parasite species and develop conservation plans.

“They may be ugly; they might be gross,” says Chelsea Wood, a parasite ecologist at the University of Washington in Seattle. “But that doesn’t mean that they don’t have as much right to exist as any other species.”

Science has a strict definition for parasites: They live on or in their host, surviving at the host’s expense. But those host expenses vary. “Not all parasites have negative effects on their hosts all the time,” says Jason Weckstein, a bird and parasite expert at Drexel University in Philadelphia. There might be cases, for example, where a few parasites on an otherwise healthy critter might be no big deal, while a ton of parasites noshing on a sick, malnourished animal could be quite detrimental.

In many cases, parasites have coevolved with their hosts long enough to reach a truce. For example, humans have coexisted with parasitic worms for millennia, to the point that the worms can manage human immunity and metabolism in ways that [might have benefits](https://knowablemagazine.org/content/article/health-disease/2025/worm-inspired-treatments-inch-toward-clinic), like countering autoimmunity or allergies. That said, in high numbers, the same worms can cause severe disease, particularly in vulnerable people like children and pregnant women.

Beyond their hosts, parasites [are members of the greater community](https://knowablemagazine.org/content/article/living-world/2018/praise-parasites). “It turns out that sucking blood and eating poo and all of the gross things that parasites do are really important functions in ecosystems,” says Wood. For example, like predators, parasites can keep animal populations in check.

By analyzing the parasites in preserved fish, like these from the University of Washington fish collection, researchers figured out how parasite populations changed over time. _CREDIT: Katherine Maslenikov / UW Burke Museum_

Consider the flatworm _Euhaplorchis californiensis_, which [cycles from snails to fish to birds](https://animaldiversity.org/accounts/Euhaplorchis_californiensis/). The California killifish it infects normally hide in the shadows. But with _E. californiensis_ in their brains, the fish venture into unprotected waters, flash their shiny scales and are promptly gobbled by birds. The parasite takes the next step in its life cycle — and keeps energy and resources moving along the marsh’s food web.

Parasite action on ecosystems benefits humans, too, says Skylar Hopkins, a parasite ecologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh. For example, parasitoid wasps inject their eggs into other insects, including hosts that eat our crops. When invasive cassava mealybugs threatened African farms in the 1970s, [introducing parasitoid wasp cocoons on land and by airdrop](https://theconversation.com/parasitic-wasps-turn-other-insects-into-zombies-saving-millions-of-humans-along-the-way-170610) saved the harvest, ensuring that millions of people had enough to eat.

So parasites are important — but scientists are largely in the dark about how they’ll fare as hosts are threatened, humans encroach on wild areas and the climate changes. “We have, just barely, the foggiest clue about which parasites are likely to be endangered,” says Wood.

She’s trying to clear the fog. In one project, her team plumbed museum collections to study 85 types of parasites found on eight fish species in Washington state’s Puget Sound between 1880 and 2019. They spotted a pattern: Populations of parasites that require only one or two host species underwent no change in abundance. But those that cycle through three or more hosts [declined by about 11 percent per decade](https://www.pnas.org/doi/abs/10.1073/pnas.2211903120), diminishing in step with rising sea surface temperatures. The authors speculate that the multi-host parasites were more vulnerable because if any one host population was altered, that could stall the parasite’s life cycle.

Wood further analyzed the potential [impact of global climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-animal-111523-102039) on parasites in the 2025 _Annual Review of Animal Biosciences_. The answer: It’s complicated. Consider the impact of pollution: Some parasites, like trematode worms, tend to suffer. On the other hand, protozoans often do well in polluted environments. And creatures known as spiny-headed worms can’t handle pesticides but thrive in the effluents pouring out of pulp mills. “There are both winners and losers in a changing world,” Wood concludes.

The IUCN hopes to protect some of those losers. While fewer than 10 parasites are red-listed now, the parasite group is investigating several candidates and aims to get up to 50 total species on their threatened list by 2030, says Hopkins, the group’s cochair. She’s careful to note that certain parasites, no matter how imperiled, will never make it onto the red list or receive protections: Anything that harms people or domestic animals is _parasita non grata_.

Knowing which parasites are endangered provides clues about what factors put them at risk. “Eventually, we want to be able to make some broader conclusions on what is going on for parasites in general,” says Hopkins.

And the red-listing will feed into conservation efforts. “We need to [piggyback parasite conservation](https://www.cell.com/trends/parasitology/abstract/S1471-4922(26)00073-5) on top of other things that are already happening,” Hopkins says. Most likely, that would mean including parasites in monitoring programs and protecting areas where they and their hosts live. When appropriate, conservationists might choose not to treat animals for parasites. Scientists might also be able to store some kinds of endangered parasites in their freezers for posterity, or breed them in captivity.

The IUCN group is already [enacting its first parasite protection plan](https://iucncongress2025.org/newsroom/all-news/new-path-conservation-first-conservation-programmes-threatened-parasites), for the Ryukyu rabbit tick of Japan. The rabbit in this case is the endangered Amami rabbit, a short-eared, pointy-faced, mottled-charcoal bunny found only on two small islands in southern Japan. It’s thought to be a living fossil that [resembles primitive rabbits](https://www.iflscience.com/meet-the-amami-rabbit-a-goth-bunny-thats-also-a-living-fossil-82083). It’s also important to the island’s forest ecosystem, spreading plant seeds and feeding dung beetles with its droppings. It’s been threatened in the past by human hunting and imported mongooses, and [remains at risk](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/16559/45180151) from feral cats and dogs and forest clearing.

The glossy brown rabbit tick sucks bunny blood, but it doesn’t usually seem to cause the rabbits harm. It might even be beneficial, by priming the bunny’s immune system.

But the tick, too, is at risk, from threats to its host plus invasive ants that eat it. Hokkaido University scientists are monitoring it, and they’ve [set up a successful captive breeding program](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/oryx/article/saving-the-ryukyu-rabbit-tick-haemaphysalis-pentalagi/CC8A9DA9A74E42DE6D81B88650FAF4F5), growing multiple generations of ticks on lab rabbits.

The rabbit tick, in contrast to the condor louse, has [become a more hopeful sort of poster child](https://therevelator.org/ryukyu-rabbit-tick/), an emblem of parasite conservation.

And here’s another reason for hope: A few years ago, Weckstein got an email from a zoo. Their California condor had lice. Would he like to check them out? Weckstein’s team is examining the samples and intends to publish findings soon.

Some posters might need an update. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: This “One-in-a-Million” Fish Has a Rare Genetic Condition That Turns It Yellow
content:
Burbot (_Lota lota_), better known as cusk in northern New England, are usually green or brown, but the specimen just plucked out of Oswego Harbor on Lake Ontario is somehow a bright shade of yellow.

It was discovered by biologists from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS), who describe it as a “one-in-a-million” catch. The yellow hue is brought on by a rare genetic condition called xanthochromism, which suppresses red pigmentation to leave yellow at the fore. It can happen in birds and amphibians, as well as fish.

**Read more: “**[**Scientists Catch a Rare Glimpse of a Fish With a See-Through Head**](https://nautil.us/scientists-catch-a-rare-glimpse-of-a-fish-with-a-see-through-head-1286577)**”**

Making the catch even more notable is that burbot usually live in colder, deeper waters. That it was found in a harbor with a maximum depth of 27 feet is unusual, though it’s not clear why or how it got lost. It’s the first time a burbot of any color has been picked up in Oswego Harbor.

The fish was found by the Aquatic Invasive Species Early Detection and Monitoring Program run by the USFWS, which looks for aquatic species that are somewhere they shouldn’t be in terms of ecosystem health. The program uses methods like electrofishing (stunning fish with electricity), fyke-netting (tubular traps), gill-netting (walled nets), and environmental DNA analysis on water samples to identify what’s in rivers, lakes, and oceans.

The USFWS crew with their find. _Credit: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service_

When it comes to monitoring Lake Ontario and other bodies of water, it’s important that invasive species can be quickly detected and removed at an early stage.

Burbot is a native fish in this area, but it continues to struggle in terms of population numbers, [mostly due to](https://hero.epa.gov/reference/6670971/) the parasitic, invasive sea lamprey. This particular yellow specimen was sick as well and taken away to Cornell University for further testing. It’s possible that its bright yellow coloring has been something of a disadvantage when it comes to sneaking up on other fish for food.

The hope is that the testing gives experts more clues about why burbot numbers remain low around Lake Ontario. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: What Goes on in Our Brains When We See an AI Face
content:
Gone are the days when we could make fun of AI-generated faces for grotesque errors like mangled cauliflower ears and an inhuman number of teeth. A steady stream of advancements now allow the technology to manufacture faces that look real. A little too real, according to a new study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1093/scan/nsag086) in _Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience_.

Psychologists from the University of Florida recruited over 150 participants—some young (18 to 37), some old (60 to 89)—to find out how their brains responded to seeing faces generated by AI. The participants were shown photos featuring either actual human faces or AI-generated faces and asked to rate how realistic they were on a scale from 1 to 10, all while their brains were scanned by an fMRI machine.

**Read more: “**[**Creating Fake People is a Terrible Idea**](https://nautil.us/creating-fake-people-is-a-terrible-idea-1285598)**”**

Remarkably, both groups rated the faces concocted by computers as more realistic than the actual faces of honest-to-god human beings. “Fake faces are being perceived as more real than real faces,” study author Natalie Ebner said in a [statement](https://news.ufl.edu/2026/11/deepfake-faces/). “You’re actually worse than just guessing, because you’re actively being drawn in the wrong direction.”

When they viewed AI faces, the participants’ brains showed muted activity in the anterior insula. Tucked inside the Sylvian fissure (the deep crease in the side of the brain), this neural region is responsible for processing untrustworthy cues. The relatively diminished activity suggests the hyperreal faces weren’t triggering any neural alarms, the researchers say.

But why?

According to the team, we perceive AI faces as hyperreal because they’re essentially an average of lots of faces. Distinctive features have been sanded off, and the result is something prototypical, attractive, and familiar—and we find familiar faces more trustworthy. In other words, AI faces may have leapt over the uncanny valley.

There was one other interesting wrinkle. Even though their brain activity didn’t differ significantly, older people tended to believe AI faces were more real than their younger counterparts. While both groups rated actual faces similarly, older adults rated AI faces 1.11 points more realistic, compared to just 0.25 points for younger folks. “All adults have hyperrealism bias, not just older adults,” Ebner said. “But older adults have it more.”

It’s not entirely clear why, however. It could be because older people tend to lean on the familiar more in general or that they’re less aware about AI-generated deepfakes, the researchers said. Either way it makes them attractive targets for scams. “Identifying that this potential deception scheme is the first step to an intervention,” Ebner said. “We can now work on awareness that if something looks too good to be true, think twice before you go along with it.”

Of course, raising awareness is easier said than done in an information environment already rife with scams. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Prehistoric Humans May Have Hunted Hippos With Poisoned Spears
content:
There’s a spot in southern Saudi Arabia where you can find seashells in the middle of the desert. Roughly 125,000 years ago, a 130-square-mile portion of the Najran Province was covered in around 100 feet of freshwater (give or take, depending on the year’s rainfall). This prehistoric lake (called Mundafan) was surrounded by lush wetlands where palms and reeds thrived, feeding a menagerie of large herbivores like extinct long-horned buffalo, ostrich, and hippopotamuses. According to a new study published in _Science_, prehistoric humans hunted these animals, and they used some surprisingly sophisticated Stone Age technology to do it.

An international team of archaeologists excavating the site found more than 5,500 stone artifacts that paint a picture of how archaic humans living on the lakeshores used the lake’s bounty to their benefit. The smooth surfaces of stone-cutting implements showed evidence of plant material like cucumber relatives and cattails, while neatly serrated edges contained “exceptionally well preserved” fibers from palm leaves. According to the team, the finds indicate the lakeside populations didn’t just eat the plants, but transformed them into other useful items, like cordage, bindings, and matting.

**Read more: “**[**Ice Age Spear Points Tell a Fascinating Story of Human Progress**](https://nautil.us/ice-age-spear-points-tell-a-fascinating-story-of-human-progress-1285384)**”**

Among the stone artifacts were over 130 fossilized bone fragments from hippos, antelope, gazelles and more, as well as over 100 ostrich egg-shell fragments. The mix of water-dwelling and dry-country fauna indicates the lake was likely surrounded by savannas. While the bones themselves didn’t show signs of butchery, the close proximity to the stone tools and the density of the find suggests they were food.

“The paleolake was therefore not simply a source of drinking water and prey but an ecological focus around which varied technological and subsistence activities were organized,” the researchers wrote.

So how did these prehistoric hunters bring down hippo-sized prey?

Per an analysis of the stone spear tips it might not have been a fair fight. On the hafts (the portion attached to the shaft of the spear), the team found residue from plant adhesives. On the tips, they found toxins from the arrow poison tree. Similar to the toxins from _Digitalis_ (foxglove), these cardiac glycosides can decrease the heart rate and may have given our prehistoric ancestors a lethal edge in bringing down the massive beasts. (Fun fact: The African maned rat also [uses](https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-14366481) poison from the tree, covering its fur in the toxic substance to ward off predators.)

It might not be the most sporting way to hunt, but it is ingenious. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Woodcocks and Snipes: The Quintessential Odd Birds
content:
We think of birds as champions of flight. Spotted sandpipers, for example, fly from their breeding grounds in Canada several thousand miles south to Central and South America in the winter. But some of their chunkier cousins in the same family (Scolopacidae) favor shorter distances. Case in point: A [study published yesterday](http://dx.doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2530196123) in the journal _PNAS_ details how sandpiper cousins colonized all corners of the world despite their less streamlined body types.

“The distribution of woodcocks and snipes around the world is really unusual,” explained study author John Bates, an evolutionary biologist at the Field Museum in Chicago. “They’re not terribly aerodynamic, and yet they’ve clearly gotten around.”

**Read more: “[How Did Birds Outlive the Other Dinosaurs?](https://nautil.us/how-did-birds-outlive-the-other-dinosaurs-1284920)”**

The eight living species of woodcocks (genus _Scolopax_) look more like footballs with short legs and heavy bills than adept flyers. Similarly, the 22 living species of snipes (_Gallinago_ and _Coenocorypha_) are stocky wading birds with long bills. None of them are migratory, yet woodcocks and snipes previously colonized islands as far-flung as the Southwest Pacific and the Caribbean.

The study authors sequenced DNA from museum specimens of 36 living species of woodcocks and snipes, plus two extinct species. Augmented with data in the [GenBank database](http://gallinago/) of genetic sequences, they acquired DNA sequences for 50 species, from which they assembled a family tree.

The results showed that over the 20 to 25 million years of snipe and woodcock existence, they’ve covered a lot of ground. Their ancestors lived in Europe and Africa, and the genetic data showed four dispersals across the Atlantic to the Americas. In fact, the birds inhabiting New Zealand and other Pacific islands turned out to be a subgroup of South American snipes, which are sisters to the now-extinct Caribbean birds. As for woodcocks, they live in North America, plus on islands in the Japan archipelago.

How snipe and woodcock ancestors traversed oceans remains a mystery. Other animals, like iguanas in Fiji, are thought to have rafted across the Pacific Ocean on floating debris. Perhaps these birds followed suit. Alternatively, they may have strayed outside their usual ranges during extreme weather events and ended up hopping/flying across the Arctic or Antarctic when it had more patches of tundra before a shift to cooler climate about 13 million years ago, according to the paper.

Once they colonized islands, woodcocks and snipes evolved into the odd football-like birds we know today. “Migration can promote diversification when a migratory ancestor gives rise to a sedentary descendant lineage, i.e., migratory drop-off,” explained the study authors.

In other words, they may have gradually given up their migratory abilities as they adjusted to island life, a trend that’s been recorded in other island bird species that forage on the ground—and, of course, many tropics-seeking humans as well. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

I’m teaching at the [Inkhaven blogging fellowship](https://www.inkhaven.blog/fall-26) again this month. In my first class, I showed off terribly-written sentences and made the fellows analyze and improve them. Some were my own miscreations, some were [Lyttle Lytton winners](https://adamcadre.ac/lyttle/), and some came from the darkest abysses of the Internet. The audience’s favorite was overwrought description of women’s breasts from erotica (one person pointed out that my PDF reader’s Recent History tab helpfully displayed porn story titles while I presented on screen - why does a PDF reader even have a Recent History tab? - so I hope my humiliation helped educate you).

But I hear that [Naomi Kanakia](https://www.woman-of-letters.com/)’s class was even spicier. She taught a course on “discourseposting”, which naturally descended into fiery discourse ([Naomi Kanakia, you are WRONG about Discourseposting!!!](https://wadapan.substack.com/p/naomi-kanakia-discourseposting), [Inkhaven Fight Club](https://wadapan.substack.com/p/naomi-kanakia-discourseposting)). I didn’t get a chance to listen, so in the grand tradition of discourseposting, I’ll argue about it without having seen the source material.

Sticking to our porn theme, and in the spirit of [The Last Psychiatrist](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/book-review-sadly-porn): one way to classify sex is through its external manifestations: positions, toys, fetishes. But another is through which psychological need it fulfills. The need to feel wanted. The need to feel valuable. The need to dominate. The need to lose yourself. The need to reenact a traumatic childhood, only this time, the Other really loves you. In the same way, we can supplement our superficial categorizations of discourseposting with the types of writer-audience dynamic that make each post exist.

In an ideal world, writers would write to convince others, and audiences would read to learn something and change their minds. But few people enjoy trying to convince others, and even fewer enjoy reading with an open mind and letting themselves be convinced. The conjunction of the two is like that murder case where the guy with the getting-eaten-by-cannibals fetish was dating the guy with the cannibalism fetish and they both, uh, achieved gains from trade. There’s nothing physically impossible about it. It just requires the conjunction of two rare types of people. Sometimes you get this in the blogosphere, and it’s great. But you wouldn’t want to sustain a national publication off of it.

I usually support taking things at face value - better underpsychologize than overpsychologize - but some of the norms and genre conventions divide more naturally by guilty motive than innocent appearance, so we can go over these in more depth. Your best bet will be to keep track of who the intended audience is (rarely the person it’s addressed to!) and what it’s doing for them.

**The Voxsplainer.**Your audience is people who already agree with you, or who are overdetermined to agree with you once they know that the issue exists (e.g. anti-corporate leftists, being informed that some new corporation is also bad). Their psychological need is for a smart-sounding person to validate their opinion and tell them that it is factually based. You’ll know you fulfilled it because they’ll say something like “I always knew something like this was true, but you put it into words so eloquently.”

**The Brutal Takedown.**The same as the Voxsplainer, except appealing to the id instead of the superego. A smart-sounding person reassures their audience that their hatred is completely valid. Nobody has ever been so hateable as their enemies. “You thought Skub supporters were slimy, but you don’t know the half of it! The latest news shows that they’re death cultists who want you to undergo constant humiliation rituals as the price of living in America.”

The Brutal Takedown combines the comfort of black-and-white certainty, with the group bonding of sharing a common enemy, with the frisson that maybe some Skub supporter is reading along, feeling angry and triggered and ashamed. It carries an apocalyptic promise that it’s _just a couple of days_ before the preference cascade starts, and all right-thinking people band together to exile Skub supporters from society forever and accord you high status for being so right about this.

**The Marching Orders:**Your audience is people who are less cool than you. Their psychological need is to learn what position the cool and powerful people support, so that they can be sure to hold it, and not end up in the scary position of taking the opposite side from cool powerful people.

They wouldn’t put it in these terms, exactly. But they forgot to develop the brain lobe that distinguishes “cool, powerful position” from “correct position”, so they need a little help figuring out what position is coolrect.

**The Virtue Signal:**Your psychological need is to signal that you’re a good person. You can’t take a genuinely controversial position wouldn’t help, because then the people who disagreed with you wouldn’t know you were good. But you can’t take an obviously popular position either, because nobody will applaud you for saying “People shouldn’t be murdered” or some similar pablum. So you need to find a position which feels controversial, but in fact is popular. Common solutions include attacking an obsolete position on its way out (“Some people say that homosexuality is evil, but I think it should be tolerated!”) a position which is popular in communities far away from yours (“Some people say we should institute sharia law, but I’m against that!”), or a position which is technically true but has such terrible vibes that nobody wants to stand up for it (“Some people say that intelligence matters a lot in life, but I believe it’s creativity which is really important!”)

Your audience is people with the same psychological need, who are less good at finding seemingly-controversial-but-actually-popular positions, and are happy to mooch off your work by agreeing that you are so, _so_ brave.

**The Revenge Killing:**Your psychological need is that somebody else has insulted you, probably incidentally while trying one of the maneuvers above. Your goal is to retaliate by proving they are more wrong than anyone has ever been before. Your audience’s psychological need is to get vicarious pleasure out of your victory, same as they would if their hometown sports team beat their bitter rival.

**The One-Level-Higher-Than-You:**Some people claim to be anti-Skub. Little do they know that anti-Skubness, as it currently exists, is _itself_ a form of Skub, a loyal opposition created to distract people from the true points at issue. Here are 86,000 words that will give you a completely new worldview which lets you transcend the Skub/Anti-Skub dichotomy and confront the people who are _really_ in charge.

Your psychological need is to look smarter than everyone else. Your audience’s psychological need is to feel smarter than everyone else. Taking one side or the other of a two-sided issue feels conformist, boring, unsophisticated. Going One Level Higher annoys everyone equally, which is almost as good as not being annoying at all!

**The Slatepitch:**Courtesy of [Matt Yglesias](https://www.slowboring.com/p/slatepitch). The Slatepitch is something unpopular yet trivial, like “Why owning a pet makes you a bad person”, or “Adultery is good, actually”. Your psychological need, as the writer, is to get clicks. Your audience’s psychological need is that they get to feel superior to it - no matter their actual station in life, they are, briefly, an Ordinary Red-Blooded American who gets to puncture the ridiculous pretensions of the elites. I [previously parodied these](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/sources-say-bay-area-house-party) with the fake publication ‘_Giving Middle-Aged Women Who Have Ruined Their Lives With Terrible Relationship Decisions A Platform To Recommend Those Decisions To Others, And People Obviously Notice The Contradiction And Post About It To Dunk On Us, But Actually They’re Only Taking Us Viral And In Fact That Was Our Strategy All Along, Ha Ha!’_ _Magazine._ Yglesias is less long-winded than I am, and just name-dropped _Slate_.

**The True Contrarian:**Your psychological need is that for some reason, you hold a belief which it satisfies everyone else’s psychological needs to beat up. On the receiving end, you get a +5 bonus to Insight, letting you easily discern all the unvirtuous and non-epistemic motives of your attackers. You have thoughts like “If only I would state my beliefs clearly and unapologetically, people would stop using me as a punching bag and take me seriously.”

Your audience is everyone else whose psychological need it is to beat you up, because now they finally have a concrete target. The virtue signaler can _prove_ that they’re not just falsely laundering a universally-popular belief as controversial. The Voxsplainer can eloquently tell people why you are wrong. The Brutal Takedown writer can grant their readers catharsis by turning you into the scapegoat for everything wrong with the world. The Slatepitcher can use you as camouflage and pretend they’re a true contrarian too. Everyone is happy, except that your “if only I would state my beliefs…people would stop using me as a punching bag” thesis gets proven more wrong than anything has ever been before.

**The Inkhaven Post:**The writer’s psychological need is that they have to write 500 words per day or get kicked out. Your audience’s psychological need is that they are your writing teacher who gets paid to read your work. The content is underdetermined by this relationship, and can be anything at all. Try to stay entertaining!

It's not obvious to me that these things are insane or harmful or anything of the sort. Obviously much depends on the details, and I don't happen to know the details[1], but:

[1] My impression is that the UK's "sharia councils" actually _aren't_ very "legally approved". Their decisions have no legal force, for instance. So maybe consider what follows as a comment on a counterfactual where there's more legal regulation/support for them than there actually is.

Suppose some group of people decide that amongst themselves they would like a particular set of rules concerning contracts and the like to apply. Maybe they should be able to have that, so long as their rules aren't too grossly incompatible with those of the surrounding state. If you and I both want me to be fined $100 any time it's proven that I've lied to you, then we should be able to make that arrangement; we could probably in fact make such an arrangement contractually and the usual legal system would help with its enforcement; but if there are hundreds of us and we all want that rule applied then there should be a more efficient way to do it than contracts.

(Cf. Scott's "Archipelago"; also G K Chesterton's "The Club of Queer Trades".)

This could be done completely privately. But if the state expects it to happen, they might prefer some more formalized arrangement involving some expertise in the state's laws and some oversight, if only to make sure of that "not too grossly incompatible" bit. (E.g., I probably shouldn't be able to agree with you to a regime in which if I steal from you then you cut my hand off.)

I'm not are all sure that this _is_ a good way for things to be. Some people who would actually prefer the rules of the state will feel pressured into using the subcommunity's dispute-resolution process instead, which is bad. There might be some degree of "venue-shopping", where whoever gets to choose whether to use state law or community process thereby gets too much influence over the result. Etc. But allowing this sort of thing doesn't seem to me at all "insane".

The “apocalyptic promise” under “The Brutal Takedown”, I refer to as a “millenarian” promise, that kind of “one final effort is all that remains to get us to utopia” shtick. Or, for the sports-analogy-minded, “overtime and we’re on the one-yard-line.”

I think it has an additional psychological need that Scott didn’t delve into which is to rally people who are tired. Most people, most of the time, are not on their first political issue. And probably a bunch of them feel like things aren’t improving as much or as fast or as well as they want. Things could be objectively improving, in the ways you most care about, and it could still feel that way! And yet rallies and protests and elections go on, and you need people to turn out even if they’re skeptical that any good will come of it. After all, if they don’t turn out, you might lose and so good probably won’t come out of it.

This is often overheated, but not always! William McKinley’s political career, which brought him all the way to the US presidency, got started on the merits of his (Civil War) military career, in which his defining moment was to - under heavy fire - bring his regiment coffee and hot food. This helped them rally for one more (decisive) charge in the Battle of Antietam. So I don’t mean to imply that this psychological need is never correct! But if your entire strategy involves a series of heroic final efforts you’re gonna burn your troops out fast.

title: How M.C. Escher’s Art Creates Bizarre Mathematical Worlds
content:
The artist had no formal math education, yet as a new exhibition shows, the insights revealed in his artwork became an enduring inspiration to mathematicians.

M aurits Cornelis Escher didn’t plan on becoming the darling of mathematicians. Born in 1898 in the canal-lined city of Leeuwarden in the Netherlands, Escher struggled with mathematics as a student, once remarking that he “never got a pass mark.” He ended up studying decorative arts and printmaking, and he used his artwork to explore the strange rules of nature that he found operating around him.

Escher saw that nature can sometimes produce impossible-seeming images. All around him, he saw distorted reflections, odd perspectives, and superimposed worlds, like the surface of a pond where you can see images of both the fish below and the trees reflected from above.

In rendering these and other visions, his artwork took on unmistakably mathematical qualities. “By keenly confronting the enigmas that surround us, and by considering and analyzing the observations that I had made, I ended up in the domain of mathematics,” he wrote in his introduction to the book _M.C. Escher_:_The Graphic Work_.

His journey among these enigmas is the subject of an exhibition entitled [_Mathematics and the Art of M.C. Escher_ (opens a new tab)](https://momath.org/escher/) at the National Museum of Mathematics (MoMath) in New York City.

Escher’s path toward math started with his love of tilings. After completing his arts education in 1922, Escher visited Granada, Spain, and was taken with the tile patterns that decorated the Alhambra. Inspired, he began to systematically study how to fill a sheet of paper with repeating shapes without leaving any gaps.

Years later, Escher’s half-brother, a geologist named Berend, sent him a paper by a mathematician named George Pólya. The paper categorized all the ways to cover a flat space with tiles, broken down into 17 groups, each with different symmetries. Escher had intuited a mathematical question, and here he had a mathematical answer.

Escher carefully traced the paper’s diagrams and studied them meticulously. Over time, he developed his own system for tessellating space, finding ways to cover a print with irregular shapes that resembled fish, birds, bats, lizards, and so on.

“He had worked out a whole theory that he called his layman’s theory, so he knew which edges had to match which edges,” said Doris Schattschneider, a mathematician and leading authority on Escher, and a curator of the exhibition.

Carolina MacGillavry, a Dutch crystallographer, took notice of Escher’s mastery of color symmetry — the rule ensuring that adjacent shapes in a tessellation are always different colors — and published a book in 1965 analyzing his drawings.

“[MacGillavry] realized that [Escher] knew more than all the crystallographers about color symmetry,” Schattschneider said. “It was something he discovered very intuitively.”

In 1954, his work was exhibited at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Amsterdam. There, he was introduced to the geometer Harold Scott MacDonald (H.S.M.) Coxeter. The two exchanged letters until Escher’s death in 1972, and these exchanges inspired some of his most mathematically complex work.

As Escher’s relationship with math grew, his artworks became more mathematically intricate, even inspiring the research of later mathematicians. But living his double life wasn’t always easy. “I’m starting to speak a language which is understood by very few people. It makes me feel increasingly lonely,” he wrote in a letter to his son in 1959.

The following images show the winding road that Escher took through art and mathematics. [_Mathematics and the Art of M.C. Escher_ (opens a new tab)](https://momath.org/escher/) at MoMath runs through February 8, 2027.

![Image 1: Black-and-white artwork by M.C. Escher depicting an impossible perpetual-motion machine where water flows uphill through a zig-zag aqueduct to power a waterwheel.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2042/11/439-Waterfall-scaled.webp)

**_Waterfall_****,** October 1961, lithograph, 15 × 11 1/2 in

Inspired in turn by Penrose’s tribar, Escher began creating worlds that used its impossible geometry. He was not in the business of optical illusions, as the writer Bruno Ernst points out in his book _The Magic Mirror of M.C. Escher_. Rather, Escher was demonstrating that drawing is deceptive. When representing three dimensions with just two, the artist can manipulate the rules of projection to deceive you into seeing, in this case, a perpetual motion machine, where the water flows in a strange loop that goes both downward and upward.

**_Print Gallery_**_,_ May 1956, lithograph, 12 1/2 × 12 1/2 in

In a feat of mathematical intuition, Escher’s Print Gallery (top) renders a static zoom. Starting from a boy looking at a print of a town, the image magnifies into the world of the print as the viewer’s gaze travels clockwise. Zooming in, we see that the town portrayed in the print contains the gallery in which the boy is found again, looking at the print.

Escher achieved this by developing a complex system of grids in which the scale of each square increases from corner to corner. In 2003, the mathematicians Hendrik Lenstra and Bart de Smit [reverse engineered (opens a new tab)](https://pub.math.leidenuniv.nl/~smitbde/papers/2003-de_smit-lenstra-escher.pdf) the mathematics behind the piece, revealing that Escher had effectively taken a complex exponential of an image (bottom). They also filled in the gap that Escher left in the center.

![Image 5](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2042/11/436-Circle-LImit-IV.webp)

![Image 6](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2042/11/Coxeter-Mobile-1.webp)![Image 7](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2042/11/Coxeter-7-scaled.webp)

**_Circle Limit IV_**, July 1960, woodcut, 16 3/8 in diameter

In 1958, H.S.M. Coxeter sent Escher a paper of his on tessellations of curved spaces. Escher wrote back saying that one of its diagrams “gave me quite a shock.” The figure showed a circle filled with rounded triangles that get smaller as they approach the edge, ad infinitum. It’s a representation of two-dimensional hyperbolic space (bottom), a negatively curved space where parallel lines diverge. The arcs in the disk represent straight paths through hyperbolic space. Escher studied this figure, tracing its arcs and determining the pattern of the circles that were implicit in it. Using what he had learned, Escher created his _Circle Limit_ series. In _Circle Limit IV_ (top), the figures take the form of angels and bats, symbols of good and evil, of which infinitely many fit in the piece.

Escher wrote to Coxeter that “not one single component ever reaches the edge. … And yet this round world cannot exist without the emptiness around it … because it is out there in the ‘nothingness’ that the scaffolding lies, determining with geometric precision the centres of the circular arcs which form the skeleton.
